column2: Is it the duty of the head lockmaster on the government canals to take care of his lock on the Sunday?
Can the lockmaster appoint one of his lock-tenders to look after the lock on the Sunday?
The locktenders, not being paid for this Sunday work when it is required from them, is it the intention of the government to indemnify them in that behalf?
Will such indemnity apply to the past or only to the future?

18996,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.1.2.2,1901-05-08,unmatched,,,,QUESTIONS.,LOCK TENDERS' SUNDAY DUTIES.,,1.
column2: The regulation as regards the care of the locks on Sundays varies according to circumstances on the several canals.
The practice of several of the canals is for the locktenders to take it in turn to perform the service, but on Chambly canal the lockmaster performs the duty.

We pay the locktenders up to six o'clock Sunday morning, and no Sunday work takes place after that hour. It has always been customary on some of the canals for one of the men in turn to keep a supervision over the lock during the day on Sunday, but for this no pay has been allowed. This duty is imposed, and has always in these cases been imposed, so far as the department is aware, without objection.
This is covered by the answers to the preceding questions.

The facts as alleged are as follows : The ship as referred to was the Canada, commanded by Capt. Arch. Conrad, belonging to the port of Lunenburg, N.S., which ship was floating the Canadian ensign, of which we as Canadians are justly proud, on the 1st day of March last past, in the port of Bahia, Brazil, when the consul of the port -suppose it was the British consul-boarded the ship and peremptorily required the (master to haul down his Canadian ensign, and threatened for such gross infringement of rules, to fine him five hundred pounds, and to hold the ship for the penalty. Such harsh treatment dealt out by a British consul, to a British master in charge of a British ship, in a foreign port, is, to my mind, exceptional. But if it is a rule that Canadian shipping is to be subjected to such treatment, by reason of a regulation, or authority of the British Admiralty, then I feel that we who are proud of our Canadian ensign, as well as we admire and feel proud of the British, should be allowed a recognition, and be permitted to float our Canadian ensign side by side with the British, and thereby have Canada treated with proper respect.

I would, therefore, ask the government to communicate with the Imperial authorities through the Secretary of State for the Colonies-Mr. Chamberlain-and have what I consider our rights as British subjects and as Canadians recognized and cared for, and be permitted to float our ensign side by side, or beneath the British, and thus avoid a recurrence in future of the unpleasant state of affairs such as alleged.
I would like to have the views of the hon. Minister of Marine on this subject, in order that I may communicate the same to the

[DOT]captain of the ship, and if it is conceded that the British consul was within his province in acting as is alleged, then a greater reason exists for a correction, and here I ask that the home authorities be communicated with by this government, and the injustice as represented and complained of remedied, in order that our Canadian merchant marine may have some certain freedom of action in the future, and be permitted to float the ensign of their country.

right hon. gentleman why it is necessary that the complainant should be required to get an order from a county court judge to bring the case into the police court ? If the provisions of this Act are not made as simple as possible, if they are not made as inexpensive as possible, and if the speediest possible trial is not afforded, the Act will practically be a dead letter. It was with the desire to obtain these objects that I presented my amendment when the Bill was in committee before. If breaches of the Alien Labour law occur ; if workingmen are to be given any of the advantages of the Act, it is absolutely necessary in their interest that a speedy hearing should be had. It is also due to the employers that if vexatious complaints are made against them these vexatious complaints should be disposed of with the least possible delay, and that the annoyance and inconvenience of having to appear in court should be reduced to the smallest possible limit. I am therefore at a loss to know exactly what the effect of the adoption of the amendment proposed by the right hon. gentleman will be. I should like to have it more fully explained. The police magistrates in the cities-and it is they who would most likely be called upon to hear and adjudicate upon alleged violations of the labour law-are well qualified to deal with these matters. They now deal with disputes between employers and employees as to wages, and as to breaches of contract and desertion of employment. It seems to me that in view of their experience in these matters they are just as well qualified in 99 cases out of 100 to determine whether or not a summons should be issued as is a county court judge, or a Superior Court judge for that matter. If persons who complain of a breach of the Alien Labour law have to go to the Attorney General of the province and get permission from him to go before a police magistrate, an unreasonable delay may take place. A delay may occur that will practically frustrate the ends of justice and defeat the desire of the workingmen to prevent cases of breaches of the law. If they have to go to a Superior Court judge it will he necessary for them to employ counsel, it will be an expensive matter, and there may be an appeal from the Superior Court judge. The same circumlocution will have to be adopted, if I properly understand the proposed amendment, even if they have to go to a county court judge. He may be out of the city ; he may be away during the long vacation ; interminable delays may take place in getting permission even from a county court judge to have the case tried in the police court. Extensive jurisdiction is given by the law to stipendiary magistrates in cities. I repeat that they are fully qualified to deal with matters of this kind. In fact I go so far as to say that from the experience they have in the class of cases that come before them, they are better qualified to deal with such a

19057,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.4.12,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,IMPORTATION AND EMPLOYMENT OP ALIENS.,,,My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has rightly apprehended the full scope of the amendment which I have introduced, and I do not believe that further consideration will change his appreciation of it. It is just as he stated. As the law at present stands, no suit can be brought except with the consent of the Attorney General of the Dominion, and that suit must be taken before a Superior Court. We propose to alter this. We retain the jurisdiction of the Superior Court but we give to the prosecutor an alternative jurisdiction before a police magistrate to have a S'wedy trial. The prosecutor has the option of going before the Superior Court or of having a speedy trial before a police magistrate. We have, however, determined that if the suit is brought before a magistrate for a speedy trial, the complainant must apply to the Attorney General of the province or to a Superior Court judge, or to a county court judge for preliminary authority.

19059,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.4.14,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,IMPORTATION AND EMPLOYMENT OP ALIENS.,,,Yes, he has that alternative. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) asks : Why do you not give the complainant the privilege of at once suing before the magistrate who has to try the case ? Well, that is a very fair objection to take and I will be prepared to hear the views of hon. gentlemen upon it. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has very well said that a magistrate, in a large city like Toronto or Montreal, is as competent in matters of this kind as would be a county judge or even a Superior Court judge. But the hon. gentleman must remember that there are several sections of the country-new sections especially -where it might be difficult to find a stipendiary magistrate equally competent with the magistrates in Montreal, Toronto, or other large centres. When this Act was passed in 1897, parliament thought it wise not to allow the party making the complaint to immediately go into court as is generally the case, but to see that some restriction should be placed upon the power of prosecuting; aud parliament determined at that time that no prosecution should be made except with the consent of the Attorney General of Canada. What was the modern idea which inspired

that disposition of the law ? The idea was that in a matter of this kind, susceptible perhaps of international complications, it would be simply an act of prudence to prevent promiscuous prosecutions, and to see that no frivolous suit should be brought. A good many complaints have been made, amongst others by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), who has always taken a deep interest in this legislation, against this provision of the statute; and I must admit that the working of the law was perhaps cumbersome, because it forced every suitor to come to Ottawa in order to obtain this permission. Therefore, we thought it advisable to extend the power of granting the permission, and we have extended it from the Attorney General of Canada to the Attorney General of the province or a county court judge or a Superior Court judge. My hon. friend would say, and with some reason, you might as well give the same permission to the justice who is to try the case. I answer that we think it preferable, in view of the possibility that stipendiary magistrates would not be as careful in some parts of the country as in other parts, to keep this important power in the hands of an officer who by the nature of his office must not only be more experienced in the law, but have a more extended knowledge of legal affairs, and who would be better qualified to exercise that important power. I do not think any serious injury or injustice or any delay can result from this permission being exercised by the county court judges; who are well qualified in all parts of the country; and I think that my hon. friend on consideration will agree with me that we have perhaps done wisely in surrounding this prosecution with this safe but after all very lenient provision.

,,,The PRIME MINISTER.,

I still strongly urge that the amendment proposed by me some time ago is one that would be found workable. The complaints that would likely be made would be made in centres of population or in industrial centres; and I think it can scarcely be fairly said that magistrates exercising jurisdiction in urban or m Industrial centres would not satisfactorily try the class of cases that would come before them, if the amendment which 1 have suggested was adopted. I must confess, however, and I do so with a great deal of pleasure, that the amendments which the premier has proposed are amendments in the right direction, and that they go a iong way to making the Act more workable than was the Act of 1897. But I hope yet that we can persuade the right non. gentleman that if he will go just one step farther and give the jurisdiction we ask to police magistrates, I am satisfied that a trial of a year or two under the conditions which we sug-Mr. CLARKE.

gest would demonstrate to him the wisdom and practicability of the amendment. If frivolous complaints were made under it the privilege could be withdrawn; but knowing the conditions of the organizations as well as I do, I say again that they would be jealous of the position they occupy and would not permit members of their organizations to make frivolous complaints, or complaints which they believed were not well founded.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Edward Frederick Clarke,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0584c1e1-b6cf-4b4b-bb53-943e8168b396&Language=E&Section=ALL
19103,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.4.58,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,IMPORTATION AND EMPLOYMENT OP ALIENS.,,,My hon. friend lias spoken upon this question from the point of view of the province of Ontario and of the city of Toronto. If the Act were only to be applied to the city of Toronto or even to the province of Ontario, perhaps I might be induced to accept his proposition. But this Act has to be applied to all the provinces of the Dominion. The jurisdiction of the district magistrates in the different provinces is not the same. Take, for instance, the jurisdiction of the district magistrate in my own province. He has only jurisdiction over petty offenders of a certain grade, and over, those of a more serious character with the consent of the accused. But in civil matters for the recovery of debts, the magistrate has onlv civil jurisdiction extending up to $100. Here you propose to give to a district magistrate in the province of Quebec jurisdiction over cases that may reach $1,000.

Now, does not my hon. friend believe, that, under such circumstances, when you give such an extraordinary jurisdiction to a magistrate, who, under the law of iiis province, has only a jurisdiction to the extent of $100, when you give him power to try cases involving a penalty of $1,000, it is a proper safeguard that there should be some authority over him to see that the case that he is called upon to dispose of is not of a frivolous character ? This consideration, I think, will appeal to the fairness of my hon. friend. I think the amendment should go as it is. My hon. friend recognizes that it is a step in what he would call the proper direction-a very long step, for my part, I am bound to say. After we had given it a trial for two or three years, we will see how it works. At the present time, I think we should go no further.

,,,The PRIME MINISTER.,

19106,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.4.61,1901-05-08,0584c1e1-b6cf-4b4b-bb53-943e8168b396,ca.m.1581,Mr. CLARKE.,,IMPORTATION AND EMPLOYMENT OP ALIENS.,,,It is contained in ' Hansard.' I will read for the hon. gentleman the amendment 1 propose :

That all the words after * fifty dollars,' in section. 1, be omitted and be replaced by the following : ' Recoverable In the name of His Majesty in a summary manner with costs, under the provisions of article 58 of the Criminal Code of 1892, before any police magistrate, stipendiary magistrate, judge of session or county court, judge having jurisdiction where the offender is to be found or where the offence was committed.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Simpson Sproule,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177&Language=E&Section=ALL
19111,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.4.66,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,IMPORTATION AND EMPLOYMENT OP ALIENS.,,,No provision is made in this Bill to meet the suggestion which is made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). If I tell him the reason is, that I do not think it is at all necessary. I am not aware, from the information I have had from the Labour Department, that any difficulty has been found in securing all the expert labour which is wanted. Whenever there has been a scarcity of expert labour, there has been no difficulty in bringing it into the country, and nobody has raised any objection to it. I may say, to the credit of the labour organizations, that in all the conferences that I have had with their representatives, they have always taken the ground that they have no objection to expert labour being brought in, if such labour cannot be got in the country. The only thing they object to is the importation of labour into the country which can be got here without going outside. The provision of the present law reads as follows :

Nothing in this Act shall be so construed as to prevent any citizen or subject of any foreign country, temporarily residing in Canada, either in private or official capacity, from engaging, under contract or otherwise, persons not residents cr citizens of Canada, to act as private secretaries, servants or domestics for such foreigner temporarily residing in Canada; nor shall this Act 'be so construed as to prevent any person, partnership or corporation from engaging, under contract or agreement, skilled workmen in foreign countries to perform labour in Canada in or upon any new industry not at present established in Canada, provided that skilled labour for that purpose cannot be otherwise obtained.
This clause appears to be sufficient to protect the labour organizations, and the employer as well, so far as my information goes.

19124,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.6.1.1,1901-05-08,,,,stagedirection,,,,On motion of the Minister of Finance, the House resolved itself into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :

That it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Finance and Receiver General may from time to time authorize the advance to the King's Printer, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, of such sum or sums of money as the said King's Printer may require to enable him to purchase the material required for the execution of orders given or requisitions made under the provisions of chapter 27 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, or of any Act in amendment thereof, and to pay the wages of workmen engaged in the execution of such orders or requisitions, before such orders or requisitions are completed and the same are paid for by the Senate or House of Commons or the department of the government of Canada giving them :
column2: Provided that the sums so advanced

column1: shall not at any time exceed $200,000.-Mr. Fielding.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W.
S.
column2: Fielding). This resolution is intended to give legal effect to a practice which has long prevailed, and which is necessary in the administration of the printing business. We have equipped a printing establishment; we have provided the building and the plant, but we have not provided what I may call for convenience a working capital. The King's Printer is supposed to receive payment from the various departments and from parliament for the work; but in the meantime supplies have to be bad and wages have to be paid, and therefore, it is necessary, that the King's Printer shall have a credit which will enable him to pay for these supplies, and to pay wages pending the receipt of his money from the various departments. This has been arranged in the past with the Auditor General, but on looking closely into the law his attention was drawn to the fact that there was no legal authority for this practice, and that it would be better that it should be made legal by a Bill in the nature of the resolution which I now propose.",,,,

19133,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.2,1901-05-08,d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68,ca.m.2854,Mr. MONK.,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,"I have no desire to offer any fractious opposition to this Increase in the number of judges in Montreal, for the reason that we are absolutely in want of additional judges in that city. But I have

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Frederick Debartzch Monk,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68&Language=E&Section=ALL
19134,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.3,1901-05-08,57ed8b95-0f38-4d6d-9502-1000823660c3,ca.m.1041,Mr. INGRAM.,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,not changed my mind from what it was when this question came up in the last parliament. It seems to me very regrettable that the two governments, this government and the provincial government, have not been able to come to some understanding as to a better distribution of the judicial work of the province. There are, as hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec know, a considerable number of our judges who absolutely complain that they have too little to do ; and it seems a pity that they should not be employed in Montreal instead of remaining to a very large extent idle in their own districts. I know that the objection to that is that this government and also the Quebec government, are of opinion that a change in the system of districts would be a very unpopular move. I think that opinion is exaggerated. 1 believe the people of the province of Quebec wish to have prompt and cheap justice, and I do not think they require, at all, to the extent suggested, the mere physical presence of a judge in any particular district. The right hon. gentleman knows that by recent legislation the jurisdiction of the clerk of the court has been extended ; so that I really believe that with a little care the districts might be so adjusted that we would be able to have those additional judges in Montreal without increasing the judiciary of the province. Nevertheless, as I have stated before, our judges in Montreal are overworked and distressingly underpaid ; and, as there seems to be no disposition to make any change In the direction I have indicated, I think it becomes necessary for us to have additional judges in the district of Montreal.

,Liberal-Conservative,,Andrew B. Ingram,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=57ed8b95-0f38-4d6d-9502-1000823660c3&Language=E&Section=ALL
19135,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.4,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,The conclusion of my hon. friend is all right, though I disagree with him in his premises. The conclusion is that we must have these three additional judges in the city of Montreal. That is imperative ; it is a necessity which cannot be avoided. With regard to the general distribution of the judicial work of the province, I must say, and I say it without any hesitation, that I have very little sympathy with the judge who says he has not enough to do. I never knew yet of the man, be he ever so busy or so idle, who could not do more than he does ; and when a man says that he has too little to do, I have little sympathy with him if he cannot find work for himself. It is not peculiar to the province of Quebec that there are some judges who have more to do than others. I do not know the province where that is not the case. The distribution of population is such that there are always some judges who are overworked, while there are others who could do more than they do. In the province of Ontario, whose system it has been suggested, I think by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier himself, we should adopt, there are many

county court judges who have not as much to do as they might do. But what are you to do ? The country will insist upon having representatives of the judicial authority at all points, within convenient and easy access. This necessitates the judges being distributed all over the province, and consequently there will be judges who will have more to do than others. That is the case in Quebec, Ontario, and, I presume, other provinces. How you are to avoid that, I do not know. However, the Solicitor General has had repeated conferences on this subject with the Prime Minister of Quebec, and we have come to the conclusion that in the present condition of public opinion, we could not change the present distribution of judicial authority and I do not know, after all, that the province is altogether wrong. My hon. friend, I am sure, would not contend that all the Superior Court judges should be concentrated in Montreal, or Quebec, and that there should be no judges of any kind in the rest of the province. If all the judges of the Superior Court were brought to Montreal or Quebec, personally, I would not object ; I would rather welcome it; but we would have to have some system whereby judges would be distributed all over the province for the easy collection of debts, the trial of petty offences, and so on ; but to leave the province absolutely without any representative of the judicial authority except in Montreal or Quebec, is a system which I think my hon. friend will agree with me cannot be enacted.

,,,The PRIME MINISTER.,
19136,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.5,1901-05-08,d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68,ca.m.2854,Mr. MONK.,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,My right hon. friend is

aware that during the past year judges from outlying districts have come to Montreal to do exactly what these three judges are intended to do, at a cost of between $7,000 and $8,000, whereas this arrangement involves an expenditure of $15,000 a year. I do not think my right hon. friend is right when he says that the judges ought to find something to do. My right hon. friend knows that there are old judicial districts in the province of Quebec in which the judge is not busy more than two or three days a month at the very utmost. Sometimes he has only two or three cases ; and my right hon. friend will not call in question, I am sure, the statement which was published in La Presse newspaper last year, emanating from Mr. Justice Cimon, that sometimes a judge found himself in his district without any cases. A judge cannot make cases if there are none ; he may devote himself to some other occupation ; and, without advocating the centralization to which my right hon. friend referred a moment ago, though I confess that the Ontario system seems to me to possess many advantages, I think we might concentrate in those districts where there is comparatively little work. For instance, the district of St. John and the district of

Beauharnois might possibly be united into one district. Some other districts might also be united. The means of communication are very different to-day from what they were in 1874. To-day a judge can go in an hour what was then quite a journey.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Frederick Debartzch Monk,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d1344229-2345-4b79-acda-cb584ec7cc68&Language=E&Section=ALL
19137,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.6,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,Let me say, in answer to the statement of my hon. friend, that judges have been brought to Montreal from outlying districts, implying that those judges could spare the time from their own districts and give it to Montreal, that I have had numerous complaints from the bar of those districts that they were neglected for Montreal.

,,,The PRIME MINISTER.,
19138,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.7,1901-05-08,06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9,ca.m.931,Mr. MACLEAN.,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,I think the House ought to pause before it praises too highly the system in Ontario. The judges of our Superior Court are not sufficiently paid, and we have far too many county court judges, who have not sufficient work to do. We .have got into the habit of increasing the number of the latter when not required, and to such an extent that it would seem they were appointed solely out of regard to political exigencies.

The hon. gentleman has spoken of negotiations between the Solicitor General of the Dominion and the Attorney General of Quebec, looking to some settlement. I hope that negotiations will also be had between the Attorney General of the Dominion and the Attorney General of Ontario, looking to some kind of reform that will reduce the number of county court judges, and thus enable us to pay our Superior Court judges better. The right hon. gentleman has found a way of relieving the strain in Quebec, and I would like to see him find a way of increasing the pay of our Superior Court judges in Ontario.

We could do with one-third the number of county court judges we have to-day. With the present increased facilities of communication, one county court judge could do the business of three counties. All members of the bar agree that on all occasions he discharged in a most satisfactory manner the duties of his high position. 19147,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.16,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,1 am sure that every lawyer in this House who has had the pleasure and privilege of practicing before the late distinguished jurist will certainly cordially approve of the proper and well-considered language in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has eulogized his memory. Coming from the maritime provinces, I take special pleasure in bearing testimony to the great reputation which Mr. King, when he was a member of the New Brunswick bench had attained, before he was translated to the Supreme Court of Canada. He was remarkable in the provincial court as in the Supreme Court for the distinguished courtesy which at all times marked his conduct towards the bar. He was a man well read in the principles of the law which he administered; and those who have practiced before him. or who, though they have not practiced before him, have read his judgments, have been well assured that the country had in Mr. King a well-balanced mind, an erudite and learned jurist, a man who at all times brought to his duties an anxious desire to discharge them faith-147

fully and well. It was the privilege of the present government, just after its accesion to power, to appoint Mr. King to a distinguished position as arbitrator for the settlement for the Berhing sea claims between the United States and Great Britain. The duties which he then discharged took up some seven months of his time; and the reputation which he gained not only among the barristers who practiced in that court and persons who had interests at stake before the court, but with the distinguished judge from the United States who became his associate and the counsel who 1 came from the United States to practice before him, was a very high reputation. To this day his name stands high not only throughout Canada, but in the United States of America in connection with the distinguished work which he so well performed. It gives me pleasure to endorse what the hon. member from Halifax (Mr. Borden) has said ; and at the same time I desire to express my personal grief and sense of loss at Mr. Justice King's untimely death. I feel that it will be long before his place can be satisfactorily filled. I only hope that the reputation he has achieved may be sustained by his successors.

19148,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.7.17,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.,,,After having listened to what has fallen from the lips of my hon. friends from the maritime provinces who knew Judge King better, perhaps, than we from other parts of the country, I may be permitted to say that I feel that we have suffered, in Mr. Justice King's death, irreparable loss. Speaking as one who had occasion, from time to time, to appear before him in connection with cases arising from the province of Quebec, I can say that though we came before him with a system of law with which he was not necessarily familiar in his early days, no judge gave us greater satisfaction than Judge King.

19153,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.9.1.1,1901-05-08,,,,stagedirection,,,,The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution

That from and after the 1st day of July, 1901, there shall be paid to the province of Prince Edward Island, in addition to all sums now authorized by law, an annual allowance of $3t),000, which allowance shall become payable and be paid to the said province half-yearly on the 1st days of July and January in each and every year, beginning with the said 1st day of July, 1901, such allowance to be paid and accepted in full settlement of all claims of the said province against the Dominion of Canada on account of alleged non-fulfilment of the terms of union between the Dominion and the said province as respects the maintenance of efficient steam communication between the island and the mainland.

He said : This resolution deals with a claim of the province of Prince Edward Island. For some years that province has been pressing upon the attention of the Dominion a claim arising out of an alleged non-fulfilment of the terms of union. This year the government of the island, by deputation and by memorial, have pressed this question again, and have urged that the government of Canada should take some action to grant the relief which they desire. Tiie province of Prince Edward Island entered the union in the year 1873. One of the conditions of the union, which happens to form the subject of controversy, reads as follows :
The Dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, viz.:
column2: Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.

column1: The contention of the government of Prince Edward Island is that that condition of the Act of Union was not complied with, and that in consequence of the non-compliance with that condition the island has been for years placed under a very serious disadvantage. The island pressed this claim some years ago, and went so far as to send a delegation from the island government to lay its petition at the foot of the Throne. Her Majesty's government at that time addressed a despatch to the Canadian government, which, without attempting to pass judgment on the merits of the island's claim, expressed a very strong hope that something should he done by the Dominion government to meet the difficulty. About that time the question of constructing a tunnel between the mainland and Prince Edward Island came under consideration, and it was thought that the construction of that tunnel might in some measure be regarded Mr. FITZPATRICK.

as a settlement of this claim. In the despatch of Her Majesty's government, allusion was made to that project, and the hope expressed that the Dominion government would take a very generous view of the matter In dealing with that proposal. As the House is aware, the tunnel project was not proceeded with, and if it was to be dealt with as in any measure a compensation to Prince Edward Island, that is of course now out of the question, for the tunnel project is not a matter of practical politics at present.

As I said, the island entered the union in 1873. For about two years an attempt was made to keep up communication between the island and the mainland by a small steamer called the Albert. I think it will be generally admitted by those who know the facts, and by those who read the papers, that the service rendered by that steamer was a very inefficient one. After the lapse of a couple of years it was felt that the continuance of that steamer on the route would certainly not be a compliance with the terms of the union,and thereupon a steamer called the Northern Light was purchased and placed on the route. The Northern Light came into the service in the year 1877, and continued in the service for some years. She was undoubtedly a decided improvement on the Albert ; but still it is contended, and with much reason, that she failed to render adequate service in maintaining winter communication so that there might be complete connection between Prince Edward Island and the railway system of the Dominion. The Northern Light continued on the service until the year 1888, when the Dominion government placed upon the route a steamer called the Stanley, a well-built and well-equipped steamer, which has rendered excellent service. The Stanley continued ou the service until 1900, then a second steamer was placed on the route called the Minto ; so that during the past winter we have had two steamers on the route rendering a very satisfactory service. Now the contention of the Prince Edward Island government has been that there has not been an efficient service as contemplated by the terms of the union, that there was not such a service until we placed a second steamer ou the route in 1900, the steamer, Minto. We have not felt disposed to recognize the claim to that extent.

The Island government have desired that this whole question should be submitted to arbitration with a view that they might be able to establish what they think would be a very large claim upon the Dominion. The claim which they made when they appealed to Her Majesty several years ago was $5,000,000. We have given the matter very careful consideration. We have to acknowledge from the data that is available that the placing of these better steamers on the route was followed by such a large business that it is not unreasonable to suppose that if

these vessels, or vessels of a similar character, had been placed upon the route at an earlier period, the island certainly would have received much more advantage from them. After very full consideration we have reached the conclusion that while the contention of the Island government that the terms of union were not met until 1900, ought not to be maintained, there was still something in the contention which the House might generously recognize. We have thought whatever might be said with respect of the services of the other vessels, that when the Stanley was placed upon the route in 18S8 and from that time forward, there was an efficient and satisfactory service ; and that the placing of the second steamer on in later years, while undoubtedly it gave the island a much better and more satisfactory service, still it is not to be regarded as necessary to a compliance with the terms of union; for we think it must be admitted whatever may be said as respects the other vessels, that when the Stanley was placed on the line in 1888 she did give that full and satisfactory communication between the island and the mainland which was contemplated by the terms of union. There would remain, then, for consideration the question of whether the island had a fair and equitable claim for failure to comply with the terms of union from the year 1873 down to the year 188S. when the Stanley was placed upon the line. It was ln. the view that the Island government might make a tolerably fair case before a board of arbitration on that point, that this government dealt with the question. We felt that instead of having the matter referred to arbitration, inasmuch as the question has repeatedly been before parliament, and as there was nothing new to be elicited, we ought to deal with the question in the way we have proposed. We have therefore suggested to the Island government whether we might not make a full and final settlement of this matter by giving them an annual allowance of 830,000 in addition to their present income. That was proposed under authority of an order in council, and the Island government have agreed to accept such a settlement, we now propose by this resolution that under the circumstances which I have stated there shall be allowed to the government of Prince Edward Island 830,000 a year in addition to their income, in full and final settlement of the claim as set forth in the resolution.",,,,

19160,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.9.8,1901-05-08,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,I distinctly recollect that some years ago when final arrangements were made with that province, the Hon. Edward Blake, then speaking from this quarter of the House, asked when we might expect a ' final finality' in our arrangements with the provinces ; and a strong assurance was given that this was being done for the last time. Every one was satisfied, and expected we were then making a final settlement of all differences between the various provinces and the Dominion. But for some time past a spirit of unrest seems to be prevalent, especially in the maritime provinces, with regard to imaginary or real claims that they suppose they still have against the Dominion. One day it comes from New Brunswick, another day from Nova Scotia, and another day from Prince Edward Island.

Now, what we are afraid of is that this is only the commencement of what must ultimately result in going the rounds of the whole of the provinces, and of readjusting these subsidies. I am not opposing this proposition, but I am only looking forward with apprehension to the time when these claims will be presented by the whole of the provinces in some form or other, and when pressure will be brought to bear upon the government to induce them to readjust the subsidies and to give something more to these provinces. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) made a statement that seemed to me to carry with it almost the suggestion that for the present Prince Edward Island ought to be fairly well satisfied. I understood him to say that another vessel was put on during the present year, and that they had succeeded with the additional service in giving steady communication between the island and the mainland.

If this be a fact, and that is all the island is claiming, providing they continue that in future, it would seem to me that they could not very well be dissatisfied. But, this appears to be a claim for losses sustained in

the past through this service not having been performed. I have always thought that there was one thing in connection with this contract and it was that we agreed to do what it was possible for us to do, and that if, through the elements, or from some cause over which human ingenuity has no control, we failed to accomplish what was intended to be accomplished, we ought to be exonerated from responsibility for the nonfulfilment of such a contract. Whether that would apply in the Prince Edward Island case or not, I am not prepared to say, but that is, to my mind, the reason why we ought to be exonerated, because we did not fulfil the letter of the contract. However, the principal apprehension I have is that this is only the commencement of a rearrangement of these subsidies which will ultimately compel us to go the rounds of the whole of the provinces and make another settlement with them.

19165,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.9.13,1901-05-08,intervention,,,,P. E. I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is drawing upon his imagination to such an extent that I am afraid I cannot answer him. I want to call attention to the principle of the proposition before the House, and to the statement made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that this was in some way or other an addition to the subsidy which the Dominion gives to Prince Edward Island in consideration of the terms of union. It is nothing of the kind, nor is it a question of unrest having recently taken place in the province, or a claim being pressed now which was not pressed years ago. The hon. gentleman has been in the House longer than I have, aud he knows very well that this has been a burning question for many years past. It is not something that has lately come to the front. He knows, that as far back as 1888, the Island government bombarded the Dominion government with memorials and petitions on this very question claiming that the contract which had been made between the Dominion and the island, at the time that the island came into confederation, had not been kept by the Dominion. This is a matter of good faith, it is a matter of contract. I have read the contract. The construction placed upon this contract by the hon. gentleman may be that we are only bound to keep up continuous communication in so far as it is practicable. It may be that the Dominion made an improvident bargain, but as to the construction he puts upon the contract, what do we find ? We find that question has been solved already. We have carried out the contract for the last ten or twelve years, which shows that it was quite capable of being carried out from the inception. There was no difficulty about carrying out the contract from 1873 to 1888, as it has been carried out since. The reason it was not carried out was simply because the Dominion government did not put on the steamers necessary to do it. They did put on steamers in 1888, and carried out the contract substantially since that time, and they did not do it before. The hon. Minister of Finance referred in general terms to the manner in which the attempt was made by the Dominion government to carry out that compact. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) knows that so strong was the feeling of unrest in Prince Edward Island that when the government, led by the present Chief Justice Sullivan and the present Senator Ferguson, were in power for eight or ten years, they not only bombarded this Dominion with memorials and petitions, but failing to get redress here, they went to the foot of the Throne and laid their memorials before Her Majesty herself. They were told that the Queen had no power to interfere between the islaud and the Dominion, or to compel the Dominion to carry out the contract which she had made with the island. But Lord Granville suggested that inasmuch as it would appear to be impossible to carry out the contract they had made, they should look with favour upon the proposal to carry out the contract by means of a tunnel. He hoped that if it were possible we would adopt that proposal. At that time, the tunnel question was discussed, ns it was supposed that we could not build steel steamships with which to carry out the contract, but since then, we have built steel steamships and put them on the route, showing that we can carry out the contract and that we could have carried out the contract previously, if we had only adopted the means that we adopted in 1888. If my hon. friend knew the loss and inconvenience to persons and property which the people of that province sustained for the eighteen years that the Dominion failed to carry out their contract, he would understand why the people have been so persistent in pressing their claim upon the Dominion government. In the first three years the Albert was placed upon that route. She did absolutely nothing. She was not a tit boat for the service, she was unable to cope with the work, and she hardly ever crossed over in that three years. The peopl^ of the island, to whom you had pledged your faith to give communication with the mainland, were absolutely without any communication at all except the primitive act of crossing in open boats. Nobody wants to have a Dominion contract kept in' that way. The bon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says that he is not offering any opposition to this proposal, but what he said, I take it, was by way of qualifying the position he took. Then, we put on ihe Northern Light. I will not dispute that when the Northern Light was put on it was a bona fide attempt to grapple with the problem, but. it was an utter failure. In 1876-7. 1877-8 and 1878-9, there were large gaps of months when the boat could not run at all. In 1879-80 for a whole month, from the 10th of March to the 10th of April, she never crossed at all. She was not a strong enough boat, she was not properly built, she was not built of the proper material, and so afraid were the Dominion government of the venture, that they actually passed an order that she should not carry mor"" than nine passengers at any one time, and an infinitesimal amount of freight. In the next year, from the 21st of January to the 25th of March, she never crossed at all. Then, in the next year, from the 4th of February to the 2Sth of March, there was no crossing.

I need not repeat them all year after year. Every oue acknowledges that the Northern Light did not comply with the compact. This is not a question of favour. This contract, which was made with the people of Prince Edward Island, was a very important contract from their standpoint : so important that most people believed there was no portion of the terms of the union which had so much influence with the people in inducing them to surrender their independence and come into confederation, as had this one. They believed that their trade would increase enormously. What was the result ? In 1888 you grappled with the question in a businesslike way. You built the Stanley and you put her on the route, and that has resulted in an extraordinary development of trade in the winter season. We only see one side of the accounts here : we only look at the expenditure, but we are apt to forget that there

is another side to that account. Last winter we carried 3,000 passengers and over 200.000 packages of freight between the island and the mainland, and we received nearly $20,000 from freight and passengers. The trade has not only doubled and trebled and quadrupled, but it has progressed in a way which has astonished even those who had the greatest faith in the development of the island when the terms of the union would be carried out. I say that the people of the island are now quite satisfied, wholly satisfied, that the Dominion is carrying out not only literally, but in spirit, the terms of the contract which they solemnly made with the people of Prince Edward Island in 1873. There is not a man on either side of politics who ever believed that there was a successful attempt to carry out that term of the union for eighteen or twenty years. The people of the island suffered greatly during that time. If this matter had been referred to arbitration, it would, I think, be admitted generally that you would have to go into court with the frank admission that you had not kept your contract, and it would be simply a question of establishing the damages. Any one who looks at the extraordinary development of the winter trade with Prince Edward Island since the contract has been carried out, will see that the losses sustained by the people when the contract was not carried, have been enormous. We now stand on a pretty fair ground, and I am glad to see that there has been no opposition so far to this settlement. As the Minister of Finance said, the facts of the case were all known to the government, and there was no necessity for referring it to an arbitration to determine them. The departments were able to give up the facts, and attached to the papers that were brought down are schedules showing the work done by the Albert-or rather showing that the Albert did not do any work-showing the limited work done Toy the Northern Light, and showing the work done by the Stanley and the Minto, and the extraordinary development of trade that followed, these steamers being put on the route.

CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,With due deference to my hon. friend, I do not see where the difference lies between giving 81,000.000 and giving the interest on $1,000,000. But, I come to the point made by my hon. friend from South Lanark. He says the contract is not at all as represented by my hon. friend beside me (Sir Louis Davies)-that the contract made with Prince Edward Island in 1873 was other than to keep up efficient steam communication, that it was not a direct bargain, but that it was qualified with the condition that we were to do the best we could, and if we found the forces of nature too'strong for us, we were not to be responsible. That is not the wording of the contract. This is it, in so many words :
The Dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, namely :

Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the Dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and railway system of the Dominion.

That is not the interpretation which my hon. friend from South Lanark gave a moment ago to this contract. It is a direct, binding and solemn undertaking that the government of Canada will maintain continuous communication between Prince Edward Island and the Intercolonial Railway. There is no provision there that the Dominion of Canada would try to do it; there is no suggestion that there might be too much ice

in certain seasons. It is true, there might be a case of force majeure. No one would complain if the service were interrupted for a day or two by act of Providence, because that is a case of force majeure. To-day there is a service which is uninterrupted except by act of Providence; but that was not the case for sixteen years. What is done to-day could have been done during those sixteen years ; but the people of Prince Edward Island, for those sixteen years, had no regular and continuous communication between the Island and the Intercolonial Railway and the rest of Canada. That was not due to the action of Providence, but it wTas the fault of the Canadian government, which neglected to do then what it has since done. Under such circumstances, can it be said that there is not ample justice in the claim of Prince Edward Island 1 The Dominion has not lived up to its undertaking, and that is the only reason why we ask tlie House to consider this claim. My hon. friend has alluded to other claims from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Those claims will be discussed, each one in its turn ; but in this case, which is so obvious, so certain, so manifest, the House should not hesitate to redeem the honour of the Dominion of Canada as pledged in a solemn contract. My hon. friend says we might have gone to the judges. So we might; but this claim has been referred to the Imperial authorities, and they, having gone into it, recommend it to the fair sense of justice of the people of Canada ; and that is the reason we make this proposal. My hon. friend from Bothwell says we made a mistake in not asking parliament to appropriate one round million of dollars instead of $30,000 a year. If we had brought down a resolution to grant $1,000,000 to Prince Edward Island, my hon. friend would probably not have supported it.

19203,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.11.2,1901-05-08,03119541-a274-44e2-ab4a-6d6f6b3c6d5a,ca.m.2710,Mr. JOHN CHARLTON (North Norfolk).,,LEASE OF RAILWAYS BY MANITOBA.,,,Before the preamble of this Bill is carried, I wish to present a few points to the committee and express the opinions, some of them at least, that I entertain with regard to this measure. It is an unpleasant position to occupy to run counter to the, wishes of many friends and to take a course which, if successful, will disappoint the expectations and desires of gentlemen with whom I have no quarrel and whose purposes I would have no desire to thwart for any rea-

son except that it is incumbent upon me as a member of the House of Commons to represent and speak for the interest of the public at large. The interests of the public at large, Sir, do not always command the consideration to which they are entitled. The masses are not here with the influences that are brought to bear in connection with legislation ; they are not here to urge their own private interests and purposes ; they are not here to ask for the friendly intervention and the friendly influence of members who may find difficulty in declining to meet the wishes of such friends. And so I rise to-night to take a position which I feel is one not entirely to be envied or desired, a position which I take reluctantly so far as it concerns the promoters of this company, who are men of enterprise and men whom I wish well-within certain limits, within the limits proper to their operations as promoters of enterprises ; but gentlemen whose purposes, if they go beyond these limits, if they trench upon the rights of the public at large, the rights of a people of a sovereign province or the people of this Dominion, are purposes which I shall feel it my duty to combat. The question before this committee is one of far-reaching consequence. It is a question that affects the interests of Manitoba in the present ; it is a question which affects, perhaps far more intimately and more positively the interests of Manitoba in the future. The province of Manitoba is not represented upon the floor of this House perhaps by as many members as it should be represented by in opposition to this Bill. The province of Manitoba, so far as the action of its government is concerned, is not represented, in my opinion, by a local government which has sought intelligently to promote the interest of the province whose destinies they have charge. I do not entertain the slightest doubt that this is a bargain marked by improvident folly. I do not believe that more than a minority of this House approve in thesis of this bargain; I do not believe that a majority of this House would stand up and affirm that the legislation that we have under consideration to-night is legislation that in its principle is conceived in the interest of Manitoba or will redound, if carried into effect, to the best interest of that province. Now, Sir, with that belief, no doubt entertained by the majority of the members of the House, I see by the records of the House-I was not present-that there were six members the other night to vote against this Bill, while there were eighty members to vote for it. I suppose I can account for the action of these eighty members, the great majority of whom believe of the Bill, probably, exactly as I do, upon the supposition that they held that this was a matter that appertained to Manitoba, that this was a matter in which Manitoba must take the consequences-if she had acted foolishly she must suffer, if she had

acted wisely she would derive the advantage accruing from that action-but in any event, whether the action was foolish or the reverse, we were not called upon to interfere in a matter pertaining to Manitoba, because this House had taken a position time and again, that it would not interfere with a province in the exercise of provincial rights. Well, Sir, that is an assumed position that does not affect me in the slightest degree, because it is based on an assumption which I hold to be entirely unjustifiable. This is not a question of provincial rights, this is not a question where the Dominion government is called upon to decide whether it will disallow legislation of a provincial government or whether it will allow it. The province of Manitoba is not here before the Privy Council of Canada, the Privy Council of Canada has not taken into; consideration the character of the legislation, it has not taken into consideration the question whether it should admit that legislation to go upon the statute-book and be of binding effect or set it aside by its veto power. That is not the question ; the question is entirely foreign to such considerations. We have a Bill before us, a part of which passed the legislature of Manitoba. That Bill comes to the Canadian House of Commons and we are asked, in a co-ordinate capacity with the legislature of Manitoba, to exercise in this matter concurrent jurisdiction. We are asked to perfect legislation which, without our action in the premises is void and of no effect. I repeat that the question is entirely foreign to any question of provincial rights ; and I assert further that it is a question, taking the phase that it has taken, in which we are just as responsible, and we are in point of fact,1 acting as purely an initiative part in this legislation as the legislature of Manitoba has done. The parliament of Canada is a party to this legislation. We do not pass upon this legislation in an appelate capacity, but we are passing upon this legislation in co-ordinate capacity with the legislature of Manitoba ; and if we pass this Bill we shall do it in a co-operative capacity with that legislature.

We had the other day a declaration from the Minister of Railways and Canals that this was a measure of almost transcendant importance, that this was a measure as important as any measure that had ever come under the consideration of the Canadian House of Commons, that this was a measure with consequences so far-reaching and so momentous that it ought not to be dealt with in a superficial or a hasty manner. I have no doubt that the Minister of Railways and Canals, in expressing that opinion, stated what was absolutely and incon-trovertibly true. Now. the Minister of Railways and Canals should speak for the government of the day in matters pertaining to railway legislation. I am sorry not to

see him in his place ; I would like to have his views upon this question to-night. I would like to know whether he, as a member ot the cabinet, having charge of the Department of Railways and Canals, thinks that this is a measure that should receive the sanction of this House. I would fain know whether it is his honest opinion that this House should sanction this measure or not. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this is a measure upon which the government cannot assume a neutral attitude. It is a measure of so great importance, it is a measure involving the direct action of the parliament of Canada, and the result of that action is so far-reaching that if there is any measure that is more entitled to be considered by the government, and more entitled to a declaration of the policy of the government with relation to it, than this measure is, I would fain know what kind of a measure it would be. I hold that in the proper discharge of the functions that rest upon the government, they cannot escape responsibility for the legislation that is being passed upon now by the House ; and that that legislation, if it is crystallized into law, would be legislation for which the people in the future must inevitably hold this government accountable. That is my opinion, and for that reason I would be sorry to see no expression of opinion from the government. I would be sorry to see the government allow this measure, possessing the features that it does, and upon which I shall enlarge later on, to pass unchallenged and without an expression of its own opinion, of its own desires, of its own views, upon the matter.

Now, there are grave considerations connected with this question. Is this Bill intra vires ? That is a most important question. If it is not intra vires we have no reason to deal with it at all ; if it is intra vires, we may go on to deal with the merits and characteristics of the measure. I believe that it is not intra vires ; I believe that the Bill is essentially unconstitutional. T do not believe that a province of this Dominion can acquire or hold railway lines which are under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government. I do not believe that the subordinate authority can rise superior to the paramount authority in this respect. I do not believe that the province of Manitoba can constitutionally guarantee the bonds of a railway in another province, as it is proposing to do by this measure in the province of Ontario. I do not believe that the province of Manitoba can constitutionally guarantee the bonds of a railway in a foreign country, as it is proposing to do under this measure in the state of Minnesota. I do not believe that the province of Manitoba can assume, as the Bill did assume, when it left that legislature, control over a railway outside the limits of the province of Manitoba, or for that matter, within the limits of the province of Manitoba. For

these reasons, among others, I believe that this Bill is ultra vires, and that we are engaged here in the discussion of a measure when we ought first of all to ascertain as a preliminary step whether our time will be thrown away, and whether we are dealing with a question that is beyond our jurisdiction to sanction, and legislation which would be declared unconstitutional.

Now, I would inquire why we should not ascertain this point ? Why not refer this question of constitutionality to the tribunal set apart by law for passing upon these points ? Why not take the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada as to these various counts and charges that this Bill is unconstitutional ? It strikes me that is the proper preliminary step to take. It strikes me that we are engaged in the discussion of a measure, that we are engaged in operations in this House which are entirely beside our proper functions, and that we are commencing at the end of the performance when we ought to commence at the head, and see first of all what our rights are, what the extent of our jurisdiction is, what the character of our measure is as regards its constitutionality. Now. if we were to take this step wp would avoid very serious complications in the future. Suppose that the government of the day had possessed prescience enough at the time to have referred to the courts the question of constitutionality upon various points connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway charter, in 1881. Suppose that the opinion of the court had been asked as to exemption from taxation. These lands have been in the legal possession of that company for twenty years, and to-day the question arises as to whether the complete period of exemption from taxation has expired or is still continuing. If we had had a reference *of this question, if we had had an authoritative opinion from the proper courts upon this question, we would have been spared all the uncertainty, and all this doubt and trouble with reference to that case. Suppose we had referred to the Supreme Court the question of the length of time that the material used in the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway should be admitted free of duty ; we would probably have had an opinion that would have convinced us that we could not admit material free when that road came to renew the superstructure of its bridges ; we would have had an opinion that the exemption from taxation and from duties upon material shall not extend till the Canadian Pacific Railway reached a time when it wanted to renew its bridges and permanent ways. If we had then referred the matter, we might have ascertained whether the Canadian Pacific Railway would be entitled to collect a dividend of 10 per cent upon watered stock that cost 25 cents on the dollar, and on other issues of stock that cost nothing-whether they would have

19204,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.11.3,1901-05-08,03119541-a274-44e2-ab4a-6d6f6b3c6d5a,ca.m.2710,Mr. CHARLTON.,,LEASE OF RAILWAYS BY MANITOBA.,,,been entitled to collect a dividend of 10 per cent on all this fictitious water and cash, in proportion of about five times as much water as substance, before the Dominion government could interfere with their tolls. If other questions in dispute had been referred to the proper court of jurisdiction at that time, it would have saved a vast amount of uncertainty, a vast amount of difficulty, and a vast sum of money to the country, and would have been in every respect conducive to the interest of the people. Now, I say that at this juncture the government should ascertain by a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada where we are, what we are doing, whether we have a right to deal with this Bill, whether we are dealing with a Bill that is ultra vires and outside of our jurisdiction. I have not the slightest doubt of this. I take ground strongly that the whole of this discussion, the action of this House, is out of place, useless, so long as we are in ignorance as to whether we have control of the question under the circumstances.

The passage of this resolution in Manitoba was marked by a very suspicious degree of haste. This contract, I believe, was made on the 11th of January, it was made public on the 16th of February, it was confirmed on the 23rd of March,'it was under the consideration of the House twenty-three days-a measure which is liable to ruin, yes, certainly will, ruin Manitoba, a measure characterized by the most monumental degree of folly, put through the legislature of Manitoba in twenty-three days, and sent down to Ottawa for concurrent action on the part of this parliament before the people of Manitoba were aware of the character of the measure.

While we are considering this measure, the people of Manitoba are considering the new features of this Bill and are arriving at the conclusion that their interests have been betrayed, and that this is a measure which could not receive their sanction. The people of Manitoba, I repeat, have had no time to arrive at an intelligent conclusion as to the character of the legislation under consideration in this House. The people of Manitoba, when this Bill was passed, and when it was sent here for our action, were as ignorant of the character of the measure as the majority of this House were when it was first brought before us, and that means that they, as well as ourselves, were in the dark as to many characteristics of this measure, in the dark as to the constitutional aspect of this case, in the dark as to the probable practical application of the measure, in the dark as to whether it was in their interests and to their advantage to sanction this measure or not. Well, the Bill has been submitted to us, and this Bill, as it came from the Manitoba legislature, provided for the fixing of rates by the Manitoba government. That was the essence of the contract, that was the inducement that
led the legislature of Manitoba to sanction it. They were to secure the control of freight rates upon the lines that this Bill had reference to. Premier Koblin, in discussing this matter, said :
We made up our minds as to what we wanted.

I stated that we wanted absolute control of the freight rates and the right to say through parliament what rates should be placed on the ordinary merchandise or produce that was carried to the markets of the world. I might say that the right to control these rates was not obtained without considerable argument and negotiation.

That was the feature of the measure that secured, first of all, the initiative action of the Manitoba government, and, secondly, the ratification of the Manitoba legislature, and if you remove from the Bill that supposed control that Manitoba was to exercise over rates, you sweep away the very consideration that secured the passage of this Bill. Now, has that been done ? It has. It has been done by section 3 of this amended Bill 103. That new section, incorporated into this new Bill, reads as follows :
Nothing in this Act or in the indentures contained in the schedules hereto, or done in pursuance of this Act or of the said indentures, shall-

column2: divest or limit, temporarily or otherwise, the rights or powers (under existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada) of the Governor in Council, or of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or of any commission or other authority, respecting any matter or thing, obligation or duty;
place the government of Canada, directly or indirectly, under any liability, obligation or duty with respect to any payment, matter or thing in the said indentures provided for or referred to;

column1: (e) authorize the Canadian Northern Railway Company to ^charge or demand any higher rates for the carriage of freight or passengers than th03e heretofore or hereafter fixed, under the authority of existing or future legislation of the parliament of Canada, by the Governor in Council, or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or by any commission or other authority.

Well, where is the consideration that led the Manitoba legislature to pass this legislation ? Where is the authority and supervision of Manitoba over rates ? It has gone to the winds. We find the explicit declaration of this very Bill to be wanting, to be gone, and we have before us a Bill that never emanated from the legislature of Manitoba. We have a Bill that makes alterations in the legislation of Manitoba in the most vital and essential particular. We have a Bill that removes the very essence of the Manitoba Bill, and sweeps away the consideration that governed the action of Manitoba. We have introduced new legislation here. We are legislating for Manitoba in the House of Commons if we pass this Bill. We have set aside the legislation of Manitoba and incorporated in place of it legislation of the parliament of Canada.

column1: Well, I do not know whether Manitoba expected this or not. I do not know whether it is proper that we should exercise this authority or not. I do not know whether we are authorized to legislate for Manitoba, hut we are doing it if this legislation passes. We are assuming the functions of a legislative body dealing with domestic questions in the province of Manitoba. We are taking the Bill which has been sent to us from the legislature of Manitoba, and we are deliberately changing it in its essential and vital particulars. We are taking out of the Bill the very core and substance, the very consideration that led to the passage of the Bill, the very thing which, if taken from the Bill, would have defeated the measure in the legislature of Manitoba. Now. did Manitoba depute to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann and to Mr. Lash the function of amending and recasting their Bills, and the right to put in new conditions in this measure which is to last for 999 years ? Were these men authorized to assume these functions ; were they authorized to legislate for Manitoba ?

19212,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.11.11,1901-05-08,03119541-a274-44e2-ab4a-6d6f6b3c6d5a,ca.m.2710,Mr. CHARLTON.,,LEASE OF RAILWAYS BY MANITOBA.,,,The great fortunes of the United States, I repeat, represent nine parts out of ten sheer public plunder, and the gains of these plutocrats have been the people's loss. One instance occurred a few weeks ago. These railway corporations control not only the railway lines, but the anthracite coal mines, and to a great extent the bituminous coal mines of the United States ; and while the price of anthracite coal to-day affords a very large profit, the combination has decided to put the price up

one dollar per ton, which represents $50,000,000 more in the shape of profits which the people of the United States have to pay to these men in the future in addition to profits already inordinately large.

These monopolies are of a character which deserve the most unqualified public condemnation. These men are public enemies. It was robbery of the petty larceny kind compared with tlieir transactions when the corsairs of Algiers levied tribute on the commerce of the Christian states, which entered the Mediterranean Sea ; and although the Christian powers rose up and put down those pirates, their operations were trivial and inconsequential in comparison with the operations of the corsairs of the present day. who compel the people of the United States to pay hundreds of millions of dollars of tribute into their coffers to swell their inordinate gains.

These are briefly the conditions that exist in the United States. Are we doing anything to introduce the same conditions here ? These great corporations were built up without the aid of bonuses, except in the case of two railway lines, the Central and the Union Pacific ; and the bonuses to these lines were secured by mortgages, which have since been paid. Such a thing as a bonus, as we use the term, is unknown in the United States. There was a system of land grants at one time, under which roads like the Illinois Central and other lines in the west were built without the investment of large money on the part of their projectors. But the bonus system was wanting. Now, we have in Canada to-day one-half the land of the North-west held up until these railways get ready to make their selections. We have bonuses granted to almost every railway project that is put afloat., We had a bonus of $10,400 a mile granted to one of the railway lines embraced in this bargain from Port Arthur westward. In addition to that, the company has the right to borrow $20,000 a mile, guaranteed by the province of Manitoba. Therefore $30,400 per mile are the ressources placed in the hands of that company to enable it to build a road that will cost over $12,000 or $14,000 a mile ; and in addition to that we propose to let them practically own the province of Manitoba. It is preposterous ; it is outrageous ; it is absurd. The practical operation of this bonus system is to open the door to political corruption ; and the conditions existing in Canada for debauching public sentiment and debauching public men are more dangerous and more likely to produce disastrous results than the condition of things existing in the United States, where the developments have reached the pitch which I have described.

Now, we want to go slowly in this matter. We want to stop and consider the interests of the people a little while. The speculators will take care of themselves. If their demands are inordinately large, if they are

column2: The dividends on this stock, paid out of the capital of the company in five years, amounted to $5,872,000 ; or the subscribers got their stock for nothing and had $892,000 besides, or 18 per cent better than getting the stock for nothing ; and that stock to-day is worth 113 cents on the dollar. We gave to this corporation a completed line of railway from Port Arthur to Selkirk, 480 miles ; we gave it a completed line of railway from Selkirk to Pembina, 70 miles ; we built for it one of the most difficult sections in British Columbia, 214 miles. We contributed towards the building of these sections $32,000,000 : we gave the company a cash bonus of $25,000,000 and loaned it another $20,000,000 and took 10,000,000 acres of land at $1.50 an acre ; and we left the company with aid amounting to $67,027,000 in hard cash and with 18,000,000 acres and a fraction of land to the good. I remember that when that contract was before this House the Liberal party resisted it and its various provisions to the death. I remember the position which I took with regard to the building of that line, and it was this. I said, we are committed to the building of that line from Port Arthur to Selkirk. Let fus go on and extend it westward up the [DOT]Saskatchewan valley, as soon as the settlement of the country requires it, to the Yellow Head Pass ; and we will then have a road from Lake Superior to the Rocky Mountains at a cost of $25,000,000, and we can then stop and consider our course for the future, and whether we will complete it as a government road or not.

column1: If that course had been adopted and if, when we had reached Yellow Head Pass, we had decided to continue that road to Vancouver in the west and from Port Arthur to connections with the railway lines in the east, we would have built the entire line for less money than we gave the Canadian Pacific Railway, and would have owned the road and 25,000,000 acres of land. Can anything more improvident, more utterly absurd, as a business transaction, be imagined than the course we pursued with the Canadian Pacific Railway-a course which made millionaires of at least a dozen

men of that syndicate, which has fastened upon this country the difficulties that now confront us, and the magnitude and character of which we are just beginning to understand-a course which has locked up great areas of land in the North-west, which has made that country tributary to this corporation, and which is held to be a reason for attempting to perpetrate the act of folly that we are considering to-night for the purpose of shaking off from the limbs of Manitoba the shackles that were fastened on them by the Canadian Pacific Railway syndicate contract. We want to take warning ; we want to begin to consider the constitution ; we require to act with some degree of business prudence. We do not want to have the capital and enthralling influence of these corporations and promoters allowed to exercise too much influence over this House of Commons.
