There can be only one of two reasons, to my mind, why the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) made such a tirade against better terms for Prince Edward Island or rather compensation for the disadvantages under which she was placed by non-fulfilment of those terms. Either he must be inspired by a very small degree of justice for the little province down by the sea, or else he has forgotten the

column1: terms under which that province entered confederation and the treatment to which it has been subjected as regards winter communication since then. It will not be denied that the bargain entered into between Canada and Prince Edward Island provided for continuous communication both in winter and summer. The words are : ' To provide and maintain efficient steam communication between the island and the mainland, & c.

This, it will not be denied, was entered into by the Dominion with full knowledge of the circumstances under which the island was labouring at that time; and it was used in 1869, and again in 1873, by the Dominion as an inducement for the island to enter into confederation, that we should have continuous communication with the mainland. This was indeed the great inducement for the island to enter confederation. Now, we know the history of how this condition has ben fulfilled since that time. In short, for the first year the Dominion did nothing to connect the island with the mainland by steam communication. In the nest two years the Albert was put on ; and it has been shown to the House that this was simply an abortive attempt to fulfil what the Dominion had bound itself to do. In the next ten years, we had the Northern Light. This vessel was not adapted for the purpose of combatting with the ice, nor was she built for that purpose, and after the first two or three years this was fully demonstrated to all who were familiar with the subject. Our delegates continually brought this to the attention of the Dominion government. But, not until 1888 did we get the Stanley, and that was the first genuine attempt to fulfil the terms of confederation. The language of the delegation that went to England on this subject-' no sufficient disposition has been shown by the Dominion government to fulfil their obligation to the island in this matter '-shows the position of the Dominion towards Prince Edward Island up to 1888. I have to dissent from the language of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he says the Stanley did fulfil the terms of the obligation to keep up communication between the island and the mainland since 1888. I contend that not until the Minto was put on a few years ago were the promises under which Prince Edward Island came into confederation in any way carried out. Nor do I agree with the expression of the Prime Minister in putting upon Providence the responsibility for the delay in the communication last winter, that delay being due to the incompetence of the department in not placing the boats at the proper points.

I have no objection to the vote of $30,000 a year being given to Prince Edward Island, but I do object, Mr. Speaker, to the agreement that this is adequate to remunerate the island for the losses to which it has been subjected, especially during the first Mr. LEFURGEY.

fifteen years after we came into confederation. The hon. members of this House must take into consideration that we are an agricultural country, and that our products must be marketed within six weeks after the crop is harvested. After that the freights are always high, nearly double the summer or spring rates ; and not only that, but our products are put upon the market at a time when, being rushed forward, our markets are glutted, and the farmers and merchants do not realize within 25 or 30 per cent of the prices they would obtain if communication were kept up for a month or two later. Now, taking these things into consideration, in estimating the loss during the twenty-five years, up to the time the Minto was put on, it will be seen that $1,000,000 will not in any degree compensate Prince Edward Island for all the disadvantage which she laboured under for all these years ; in fact, it seems to me a very small sum indeed compared with the losses that the island has suffered. I wish to place myself on record as dissenting from the view of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the agreement of the local government of Prince Edward Island, in accepting $30,000 per annum as full recompense for all the losses which the island has suffered through the failure of the Dominion to carry out the terms of confederation.

On the subject brought forward by the hon. member from Toronto of the very unpopular, and, to almost all the commercial and industrial people of Canada, iniquitous tax imposed on commercial men by the Liberal administration of Prince Edward Island, I have to say that it is, to my mind, detrimental to the best interests of our people, and contrary to the spirit of that free commercial intercourse which should exist between all parts of this fair Dominion. I trust that the present provincial government will see fit to have this method of extracting blood money expunged from our statute-books, as it stands a menace to our commercial standing.

Mr. JAMES ,T. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) During the discussion upon this resolution this afternoon, I was surprised at the misapprehension that seems to exist in the minds of some hon. members in this House, and particularly in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite, if the views expressed by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and. especially by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), are to be taken as a criterion of the views of which hon. gentlemen opposite hold. I was surprised, and new members of this House might well be surprised, that an hon. gentleman of the standing in this country of the hon. member for South Lanark, a gentleman who held the position of a cabinet minister in a former government, and who, if the Conservative party had been successful in the last general election, would, in all probability, be a cabinet minister now,

should exhibit such a lamentable want of information on a question of such importance as this, as was exhibited by that hon. gentleman. Any one who has read anything of the histoi'y of confederation knows that the province of Prince Edward Island remained out of the union for several years after the larger provinces were confederated, and that during that time negotiations were continually going on between the Do-' minion government and the government of the island, with the object of inducing Prince Edward Island to join the union. No argument was held out that formed such a strong inducement to the people of Prince Edward Island to join the union as this- that if they did so their isolation would be removed, they would be no longer subjected to the disadvantage that their insular position entailed upon them, that they would be placed in efficient and continuous communication with the mainland. This was the inducement above all others that caused the government and the people of Prince Edward Island to entertain the terms of the union and join confederation. And so important did the people consider this matter, and so important did their delegates consider it, that there was no doubt whatever in the terms that were laid down in the contract of union. This is what the Dominion undertook to do :

To establish and maintain efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers between the island and the Dominion winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial Railway and the railway system of the Dominion.

It appears that hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly the two I have named, regard this payment to Prince Edward Island as a rearrangement of the terms of confederation, an increase in the subsidy. It is simply and solely a payment to Prince Edward Island for damages sustained through nonfulfilment of the terms of union for several years. The hon. member for South Lanark, maintained this afternoon that the terms of confederation were carried out-I think he said were carried out in the spirit and the letter-at all events, that was the meaning of what he said. To show how far this is from the facts of the case, I will state the facts, and hon. gentlemen can draw their own conclusions. .For the first year after confederation, no attempt at all was made to carry out the terms of union in this respect. For the next two years the communication was simply a mockery. An old wood boat which, when originally constructed, was not intended even for summer navigation, was placed upon the route. She, of course, lamentably failed. Then, in 1876, the Northern Light was purchased and put upon the route. The Northern Light was not designed for the service at all, she was designed for the River St. Lawrence; and every one knows that the winter navigation of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the Straits 148
column2: [DOT]

column1: of Northumberland cannot be compared with river navigation. The Northern Light did not fulfil the terms of confederation, did not give continuous or efficient communication with the mainland during any period of her history.

Now, another mistake under which I am sorry to see hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House appear to be labouring, is that these terms which the Dominion government made in the province of Prince Edward Island were entirely in the interest of the island. That is not correct. They were no doubt in the interest of Prince Edward Island, but they were also in the interest of other provinces as well with which Prince Edward Island traded. If it was profitable for Prince Edward Island to trade with the maritime provinces, to trade with Quebec and Ontario, it was also profitable for these provinces to trade with Prince Edward Island ; because all trade must be mutually profitable or it will cease to exist. We had an illustration of that this afternoon in the telegram that was read by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke), where an association of commercial travellers protested against the per capita tax that was levied upon these men when they came to Prince Edward Island to sell goods. In that telegram they stated that the imposition of this tax would be an injury to the trade and commerce of Ontario, showing that Ontario has a profitable trade with Prince Edward Island. Anything that is done to facilitate trade and travel to and from that island is beneficial to the other provinces. Therefore, the money that is spent in keeping up this trade and carrying out the terms of union, is not entirely to the advantage of Prince Edward Island, but is an advantage to all the other provinces as well.

Now, I have gone over the first three years of confederation, from 1873 to 1876, to show that no effort, practically, was made to carry out the terms of union. In 1876 the Northern Light was purchased and put upon the route. But she was not designed for that service, and consequently she became a complete failure. So great was the failure that she was unable to perform the service at all for about seventy days each year during the whole time she was on the service. In 1881, I think it was, she was icebound for so long a period that the crew and passengers, despaired of reaching land. Among the passengers were several women and children, and the provisions running short on board, they undertook to walk from the vessel, a distance of several miles, to land. Night overtook them, and they were subjected to so much cold and exposure that one of the party lost his health and shortly afterwards died. Another of the party was crippled for life. Now, will the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) say that this was continuous and efficient communication with

the mainland ? In 1884 a party of twenty-two men undertook to cross by the old method in an open boat, a method that was In vogue fifty or sixty years before the island joined the confederation. The movements of the Northern Light were so uncertain that they preferred to cross that way to depending upon the steamer. A snowstorm came on, night overtook them on the ice, and they were out for two days and one night. Every member of the party suffered from the exposure, and several of them had to undergo amputation of their limbs. Now will the hon. member for South Lanark say that this was carrying out the terms of confederation ? Was this placing us in communication with the Intercolonial Railway and with the railway system of the Dominion '?

The committee of parliament further recommended that, inasmuch as the evidence taken before them went to show that the Northern Light was fast becoming unfit for service, another suitable steamer should be provided to take her place.

Well, another suitable steamer was not provided for live years after that, and yet in face of this testimony it is said by hon. gentlemen that the terms of confederation were carried out. As the Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated this afternoon, so impressed was the government of that time with the inadequacy of this boat, with her unseaworthiness, that an order was issued from the Department of Marine and Fisheries limiting the number of passengers that she was allowed to take on any one trip. Now, Sir, do you think, in view of all these difficulties I have narrated, that the communication then provided was conducive to trade and travel between the province and the mainland ? I myself crossed over from the island to the mainland in 1881 or 1882, and no man who has not crossed there by these boats has any idea of the hardships to which we were exposed. None but the strongest and most robust men would undertake the passage, none but people who were compelled by some grave reason would undertake it at all. They had to be strapped to the boat, so that if they fell overboard, as was a frequent occurrence, they could be dragged up again by some of the other passengers or crew.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.)

Now, while provision was made for carrying the mail in this antiquated way, no provision was made by the government for bringing passengers across even in open boats. The passengers had to pay whatever fare was demanded, and to work their own way. Then when they got to Cape Tormentine they had to drive forty miles, over the winter roads, in open sleighs, to Amherst, before they could make connection with the Intercolonial Railway. It was provided in the terms of the union that from the date of union, efficient and continuous steam communication, winter and summer, should be preserved between the island and the mainland. But, will any man who will read the history of this question say that the Dominion government maintained the terms of the bargain ? They did not even do as was recommended by this committee in 1883. The committee recommended that when people were obliged to cross in an open boat, houses should be built on each side of the straits, so that when passengers got to their destination they might have some place to which they could go and warm themselves and change their clothing ; and that there should be on each side some place where boats could be hauled up and put under cover, and be in a fit condition to commence the service the next day. Although that recommendation was made in 1883 by a parliamentary committee, it was not carried out. There was nothing done in that respect for three years afterwards. This is what Sir Alexander Campbell, speaking in the Senate in 1884, said :

I am surprised to hear from my hon. friend opposite that the boat-houses have not been built. I called the attention of the Minister of Marine (Mr. McLelan) to the matter last session, and he told me that the boat-houses would be provided. I shall again call his attention to that question, and to the various suggestions that have been made.
That was in 1884. In 1885, the next session the same gentleman said:

My hon. friend from Prince Edward Island, who introduced this subject to the notice of the House, has, I think, just ground for complaint, ground for complaint, I am sorry to think, perhaps against myself, although really, as he has almost admitted, I am not responsible for the non-execution of the measures which, from time to time, I have been authorized by the government to promise in this House. I remember quite distinctly the undertaking which I gave that the boat-houses should be constructed, one on each side of the ferry. I made that promise with the authority of the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and as is my constant practice, the very day the promise was made, I wrote to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, pursuant to what he had told me, I made the promise, and that I hoped he would keep it in mind. I afterwards called attention to it, and there were reasons which were more or less sound'-I can hardly say sound -which made the delay more or less excusable. It was thought for a time that the orders had
been given, and that the boat-houses were in course of construction.

For three years after the promise had been made and after the necessity had been pointed out by the parliamentary committee, no boat-houses had been erected, nothing was done to improve the crossing of boats there and the conditions remained the same as they had been for several years before the island came into confederation. Up to 1888, when the Stanley was constructed, no proper, bona fide attempt was made to carry out the [DOT]terms of union in this respect and consequently Prince Edward Island had, by every rule of equity and justice, a claim against the Dominion government for the non-fulfilment of the terms of union. There is no question that the people of the island suffered very severely in consequence of this matter. As has been pointed out already in this debate, the people of Prince Edward Island were obliged to send their agricultural products to the provincial markets during a short time in the fall of the year when the markets were at their lowest. They had no communication with the mainland during the winter. The merchants were obliged to import all the goods wanted for five or six months ahead, in the fall and to pay interest on this large importation. If you want to fully realize what the island did suffer on account of the non-fulfilment of these terms you have only to turn up the records of traffic that have been made since the two isteamers were put on this route. The trade of the island has been so great, that, as the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries showed here to-night, it has gone on developing and increasing every year since an honest effort was made to carry out the terms of the union. We have still further proof that this effort has developed and increased our trade. Last year the net earnings of the Prince Edward Island Railway, in consequence of the facilities that were given to trade with the other provinces of the Dominion of Canada during the winter season, were 87,000 and over greater than in any other period of the history of this railway, and this year, in consequence of the two steamers being put on the route and greater facilities being supplied, the net earnings of the railway will be between $15,000 and $20,000 greater than the year before. The net earnings of the Prince Edward Island Railway will, if they go on increasing as they have been increasing during these last two years and as they are likely to continue, will return to the exchequer of this country an amount equal to the amount we are how placing to the credit of that province, so that as a financial transaction the Dominion of Canada will lose nothing whatever. If the net earnings of the Prince Edward Island Railway go on increasing as they have increased since the facilities for trade have been improved, they will in a very few years represent the full amount of the $30,000 additional subsidy or payment 148*

that we are giving to Prince Edward Island. So that in that respect alone the Dominion of Canada will lose nothing by the transaction. That shows clearly that when the Dominion government provides facilities for the trade and commerce of the country between the different provinces and between Canada and other countries, it is pursuing a good policy, a paying policy, and a policy that will always give an adequate return directly and indirectly to the people of the country. If the earnings of the Prince Edward Island Railway were $7,000 greater last year than in any previous year, and if this year they will amount to $15,000 or $20,000 more than they were last year, it will give hon. gentlemen an idea of the loss that the province sustained during the sixteen or eighteen years when these facilities, which were stipulated for in the terms of union, were withheld. I am sorry to think that there should be any sectional difference in this matter. I trust that the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) does not voice the opinion of many hon. members from Ontario on the other side of the House. I hope and trust that this resolution will pass the House by a very large majority. I believe that the government of this country is to be congratulated upon having settled this question fairly and equitably, and I believe that parliament will ratify that settlement, and that hon. members from Ontario, from the west and from the maritime provinces will admit that it is a fair and reasonable arrangement. Perhaps it may be thought by some hon. gentlemen that this is a new question, that it has only been brought up now or since the present government came into power, but such is not the case at all. From the year 1881, right along to the present time the government of Prince Edward Island have memorialized and petitioned, time after time and year after year, the Dominion government upon this question. Wearying and despairing almost of getting any redress of their grievance, as it was pointed out this afternoon, they carried the matter to the foot of the Throne and so impressed the justice of their claim upon the Colonial Secretary Lord Granville, that although he stated that the Imperial government had no authority to interfere in the matter he suggested that the Dominion government should undertake the building of a tunnel beneath the Straits of Northumberland at an expenditure of $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 in order to overcome the difficulty of carrying out their agreement in this respect. The people and the governments of Prince Edward Island never allowed this matter to rest, although the government that had been in power from 1878 right along for many years did nothing more than make a bare acknowledgment of the memorials and petitions that were sent to them. But, the people of Prince Edward Island hoped for the time when a government would be in power in Canada that would do them justice

in this matter, when a government would be in power to which they might appeal with confidence. Well, they have appealed, and they have brought this matter before the present government, and X am proud and glad to be able to say that the appeal has not been in vain. I believe that the government has considered the matter fairly, reasonably and equitably. It may be, as my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) stated, that the amount is not sufficiently large, but I believe that the government have taken a fair and reasonable view in the matter and that they did what they believed to be fair in the interest of not only of Prince Edward Island, but in the interest of the people of Canada as a whole. I believe that this parliament, endorsed by the people of the Dominion, will ratify this agreement. I hope and trust that when the vote is taken a large majority of the members of the House will support the proposal; indeed I hope that the House will be unanimous in its favour.

CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,I am not prepared to give an opinion upon the merits of this question, but I assume that Prince Edward Island would not be demanding this extra subsidy from the Dominion, if its revenues were sufficient to keep pace with its expenditures. The question of subsidies for the provinces will in the future be one of very great importance, and will be a question with which the government of this Dominion shall have to deal. If one province, with a population of 100,000 requires an extra subsidy of $30,000 per annum, and makes out a fair case for it, then it is a very simple mathematical problem to discover how much additional subsidy will be required for a province with 2,000,000 inhabitants, which also makes out a fair case. This question is one of very great importance as I have said, and it will no doubt have to be solved by this or by some future Canadian government. I would like to emphasize the point raised by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The letter which he read from the president of the Commercial Travellers' Association shows that the rest of the Dominion has a real grievance against the people of Prince Edward Island on account of the attitude which it has taken towards the trade of the other provinces. This House may perhaps be guided to some extent in considering this matter by an editorial which appears in to-day's Toronto Globe, a paper which cannot be accused of trying under any circumstances to embarrass the present government. I shall read the following extract from the article in the Globe :

Prince Edward Island, the smallest province in the Dominion, has put forth a strong plea for an addition of $30,000 to its annual subsidy. The outlay of the province seems determined to overtake and pass the revenue, a situation by no means unique in governmental affairs. When the increased subsidy is under consideration, with a prospect of generous treatment, it
Mr. HUGHES fKing's, P.E.I.)

would be a gracious and at the same time a profitable thing for the province to abandon the system of disguised protection maintained against the rest of the Dominion. The local legislature now levies a tax of $15 a year on all commercial travellers doing business in the province, and as soon as a traveller lands at Charlottetown he is a mark for the collector. They should make their markets as free as possible to the trade of the Dominion. Let Prince Edward Island show more intelligent selfishness and collect its revenue by methods that do not discourage commerce, do not take more from the people than goes into the treasury, and do not stir up. a feeling of antagonism in other provinces. Local protection policies by towns and cities are now thoroughly discredited, and no province should seek to exclude the trade of the Dominion.

At any time within the last few years visitors to the island province became at once subjects of suspicion. They were tracked by detectives and if they went there to do business, unless they handed over this $15 tax, they were summoned before the courts. The matter in itself may appear small but it should be remembered that this tax is imposed in the different towns and especially in Charlottetown. It is a mode of taxation which has been discarded all over the world. The city of Quebec some years ago endeavoured to impose such a tax, but the legislature refused to allow it. The people of the other provinces desire to transact business with their fellow-countrymen in Prince Edward Island, and they should not be hampered by this antiquated restriction on trade. The trade between Prince Edward Island and the other provinces should be on the same footing as the trade between Ontario and Quebec, and the trade between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. If the Minister of Marine (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) were in the House to-night, I would ask him to bring his influence to bear on the people of Prince Edward Island to do away with this obnoxious taxation which they impose on the trade of the other provinces. But in the absence of the Minister of Marine, I appeal to the right hon. leader of the government and to the representatives from Prince Edward Island to use their influence in that direction. This tax is not in force in any other part of the Dominion, and I trust that our friends in Prince Edward Island will soon abolish it, and get into line with modern methods of doing business.

Hon. Wm. ROSS) (Victoria, N.S.). I entirely endorse the remarks of the last speaker (Mr. Kemp). I believe that there should be no restriction of any kind; on trade between one part of the Dominion and another. We who profess to lean towards free trade ought to feel ashamed that there should be a province in the Dominion which would levy a mean tax of this kind. I shall not detain the House at any length, but before touching the main question, X wish to say that I have listened with great pleasure to the remarks of my hon. friend from Guyshorough (Mr. Fraser) ; and since he has referred to me, 1 can assure him that for the last twelve years I have continually raised my voice against this tax on commercial travellers. But why was my voice not listened to ? Because the friends of the hon. gentleman, a Liberal government, were in power in the province. I would be only too happy to have that tax repealed. It is an obnoxious tax-a tax on the trade of the country. It is not a municipal tax, but a tax imposed by one province against other provinces. If the city of Charlottetown, or the town of Summerside, had imposed a municipal tax on commercial travellers, we could not object so much, but it is the hon. gentlemen's friends who imposed this obnoxious tax against the commerce of this country. I trust that the right hon. the First Minister will urge the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, who I regret is not in his place, to use his influence with the local government to have this tax repealed during the session now being held on the isalnd. The wholesale dealers in the cities of Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, St. John, Quebec, and other parts of Canada, send their travellers to our province. These men spend their money there. They pay their fares on the railways, they pay their hotel bills. If they want to be driven out into the country they hire the farmers horses, and they leave their money in the province, and it is not fair to treat them in this way. It is not so much the amount of money raised that is irritating as the way in which this tax hampers business, detectives being put on the tracks of the traveller, as the hon. gentleman has said, the moment he sets his foot on our shores. The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock), who is a wholesale merchant, tells me that he sends four men to the island twice a year to sell goods, and it is in the interests of the island itself that this trade should be untrammelled, and this blot upon
the fair fame of the province be wiped out, and I trust that hon. gentlemen opposite will impress on their friends the necessity of having that done.
I would not have risen to address the House but for the remarks made by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart), and the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean).

The resolution before the House does not call for an increase of subsidy, but simply for compensation to the people of the island for the non-fulfilment of the terms of the union. The right hon. the First Minister touched the gist of the question when he said that governments as well as individuals should carry out their contracts. It has been shown that the government of Canada had not fulfilled its contract in this respect, that while they undertook to maintain continuous steam communication, winter and summer, between the island and the mainland, they failed to do so. The hon. member for Lanark was in this House and a member of the government which, in 1887, placed upon the statute-book an Act giving Prince Edward Island in perpetuity $20,000 per year, on the ground that the island was called on to contribute towards the subsidizing of railways in other parts of Canada, which were of no advantage to her. We find, therefore, a precedent in the policy of a Liberal-Conservative government for the course we are pursuing to-day. When that government believed that an injustice was done, they passed an Act placing in perpetuity to the credit of Prince Edward Island this sum of $20,000.

This government is simply repeating what *was done by their predecessors. After careful scrutiny, they find that this money is due to the people of Prince Edward Island. A need not go into the subject of the great loss entailed upon Prince Edward Island because of the want of communication for so many years-that has been gone into fully by my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr Lefurgey) and also by my hon. friend from King's (Mr. Hughes). This is a simple act of justice. It is not altogether in the interest of Prince Edward Island. The letter from the Commercial Travellers' Association, which was read by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), will show that the people of Ontario are also deeply interested in this question of steam communication. The claim was made, as stated by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that $5,000,000 should he paid to Prince Edward Island to compensate for the want of this communication. The government were willing, it appears, to pay $1,000,000. I am glad that they have recognized to a certain extent the rights of the province, and I hope that not only in this matter but in others, the Dominion will be willing to do justice to the people of Prince Edward Island, who are called upon to contribute their share of taxation as one-

fortieth of the population. We accept this as a moiety of what is due us, hut we cannot take it as a full settlement. The Minister of Finance, as well as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, stated that the service since the Stanley was placed upon the route in 1888 was a very satisfactory service and that there was no dissatisfaction with it. I desire to tell the horn, gentlemen that there is dissatisfaction, though the Dominion has placed two boats there. I will not say that an honest effort has not been made since 1888 to carry out the terms of confederation. Still, great dissatisfaction prevails in the province of Prince Edward Island. I had the privilege of bringing to the attention of the House the fact that for ten days this winter the province of Prince Edward Island had been without communication. with the mainland. Can this be called a satisfactory state of affairs ? We must persist in our protest until these boats are placed at the right points, in order to assure the maintenance of communication. Where are the right points ? As I stated here before, the government should keep the Minto on the route between Georgetown and Pictou, at the eastern end of the province, and the Stanley between Summerside and Cape Tormentine, at the western end of the province. If you keep the two boats at one point, they are likely to be blocked, as they were for ten days this winter. I wish to impress upon the right hon. the Prime Minister that to maintain this communication, the pier at Cape Tormentine should be placed in proper condition for the handling of freight, and then have the boats run as I suggest. When the wind blows from the east and blocks the eastern route, it will clear up the western ; and when it blows from the west, threatening the possibility of blocking the j western route-though this has not resulted this winter-it will open the eastern passage. I shall not enter into this contract which was made at the time of the union ; that has been gone into fully. Men of great experience on both sides of politics, made that agreement under which the Dominion was to maintain communication winter and summer between the island and the mainland. Canada failed to carry out that contract in the past, and I fear that unless my advice is taken by the government, they may fail in the future. If they do fail, we shall feel it our duty to press for the recognition of our rights. My hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) spoke of this as an increase of subsidy. The day may come foreshadowed by the hon. gentleman when we must have a general house-cleaning with regard to these subsidies, and a new start. When the province of Prince Edward Island entered into confederation, it was believed that the subsidy, together with a small tax imposed on the people, would be sufficient to carry on the affairs of the government for all time. That has Mr. HACKETT.

been found not to be the case. We have no resources except in our agricultural lands and fisheries ; we have no mines or timber to fall back upon ; and if our revenue fails, our only recourse is to a direct tax. The other provinces have great resources such as we have not. Consequently, it is the duty of the government of Canada, I care not which side of politics it may represent, to look carefully into this matter and see that justice is done to the people. Now, I saw a statement in a newspaper that Ontario was the great milch cow of the Dominion and that the provinces down by the sea were milking her dry. But what are the facts ? I had the honour of having a seat in this House in 1880, when the question of building the great Canadian Pacific Railway came before parliament. I favoured the proposal. We in Prince Edward Island faced the non-fulfilment of the terms of confederation, and there was a claim from British Columbia also that in their case the terms of confederation were not carried out. The people of Prince Edward Island, living a thousand miles east from Ottawa, contributed their equal share for building that railway. There is no province in Canada that has derived such great advantage from the building of that railway as the great province of Ontario. From Lake Nipissing to Port Arthur, a distance of 800 miles, through the province of Ontario, that railway traverses a region that was then unknown not merely to the people of Prince Edward Island, but to the people of the province of Ontario. The building of that railway has opened up the country now known as New Ontario, a country rich in mineral and timber wealth. It is considered a great thing to give the people of Prince Edward Island this $30,000. But they have contributed their share toward the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Ottawa to Vancouver, from which they derive no direct advantage. Let us be just in carrying on the affairs of the country. Whatever party may be in power, what we want is fair-play.

Now with regard to the running of these steamboats, you may consider that the sum of $30,000 is a large amount. My hon. friend from King's (Mr. Hughes) has shown the increase in the revenue on the Prince Edward Island Railway, which is owned by the government, by reason of running these boats in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. You will find in a few years that, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries stated this afternoon, the revenue derived both from the railway and the steamships will be quadrupled ; and this money that you think you are paying to the province of Prince Edward Island will be returned to the people of the Dominion by the increased earnings of the railway and steamships. I trust, therefore, we have heard the last of this sectional cry that Prince Edward Island is receiving more than her rights. I
hope this resolution will be passed unanimously. There should be no vote upon it. I say again that we accept this money as a part of what is due us because of the nonfulfilment of the terms of union.

The opinion of L'Evenement on the question of Federal subsidies : The Patrie believes that the resolution which has just been reached by the Laurier government of increasing by $30,000 the annual Federal subsidy to the Island of Prince Edward is probably the first step in '.he way of the readjustment of the subsidies to the provincial governments.

As I said before, we are now opening the door to the presentation of claims for readjustment and the result will be that the time of the House for the next five years will be taken up in discussing these claims

from the different provinces for better terms. I, for my part, protest against it, not because I think Prince Edward Island should not have justice done to her, but I protest entirely against the way in which it is being done and against the way in which the government have raised this question.

,Independent Conservative,,William Findlay Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9&Language=E&Section=ALL
19242,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.12.26,1901-05-08,74dd6652-cc90-4645-97e9-bfadb4e237e7,ca.m.6207,Mr. DAVID HENDERSON (Halton).,,P.E.I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,Mr. Chairman, a good deal has been said by some hon. members from Prince Edward Island in the way of showing that Prince Edward Island has not received its fair share from the Dominion. Now it seems to me that in the past Prince Edward Island has been very fairly treated indeed by the Dominion parliament. We find that at confederation and every year since the province of Ontario received an allowance of $80,000 for government purposes under the British North America Act. The province of Prince Edward Island with a population of only 109,000, whilst the province of Ontario has a population of about 2,000,000, received the sum of $30,000. If the province of Ontario had received for government purposes in the same proportion as was meted out to the province of Prince Edward Island, she would have received, I dare say, about $600,000. I mention this to show the fact that Prince Edward Island has all along, ever since she came into confederation, been receiving, pro rata, nearly $30,000 a year more than she was entitled to receive on the same basis as this allowance was made to the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, so that, if $30,000 a year is a fair basis of settlement now for the loss that. Prince Edward Island has sustained during the fifteen years from 1873 to 1888, I say that Prince Edward Island has already been compensated and compensated fully for this loss. I have no doubt whatever that $30,000 is abundant to meet the loss which has been sustained by Prince Edward Island on account of the non-fulfilment of the conditions entered into at the time that the island came into confederation in relation to the keeping up of communication between the province and the mainland. I say that I have no doubt that $30,000 a year is abundant. I do not know the data upon which this calculation as based. The papers are to be brought down and we will have an opportunity of reading them, perhaps, before the final reading of the Bill based upon this resolution takes place and of finding out something more as to how this figure was arrived at. I have no doubt from the fact that we have this afternoon heard the statement of the Hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Sir Louis Davies), who comes from the island and who appears to be fully satisfied that $30,000 is adequate compensation, and from the other fact that not only the money consideration but the political consideration has to be satisfied, that this amount is sufficient.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,David Henderson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=74dd6652-cc90-4645-97e9-bfadb4e237e7&Language=E&Section=ALL
19243,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.12.27,1901-05-08,06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9,ca.m.931,Mr. MACLEAN.,,P.E.I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,They seem to regard it as sufficient, I believe in this matter that the political consideration is possibly as important a factor as the equity consideration that is being given to Prince Edward Island. What the government no doubt want to do is to conciliate the people of Prince Edward Island by giving them a sufficient sum of money to compensate them for their loss and they would never think of making a settlement which would fall short of that and which would leave the people of Prince Edward Island dissatisfied. Whilst they want to conciliate them with a full money consideration for their loss, they want to make it ample to be sure that the people of Prince Edward Island will not be a disappointed factor in any political question which may hereafter come up. Now I have shown that whilst Prince Edward Island has been receiving for government purposes $30,000 a year every year since it came into confederation, the province of Ontario has only received $80,000 a year and the province of Quebec $70,000 a year for the same purpose, so that, practically, the province of Prince Edward Island has received nearly $30,000 in excess of what she would have been entitled to if this allowance had been made pro rata according to the population of the different provinces. But I find that in regard to the allowance per head of the population of 80 cents, given to each of the provinces, Prince Edward Island receives her subsidy based on the population at the end of each decade. She is now being paid at the rate of 80 cents per head on the population of 1891, while the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec, the provinces which pay the larger part of this money, are only receiving their subsidies of 80 cents per head on the basis of the population in 1861. You see again that the province of Prince Edward Island has a decided preference in the subsidies that are given by the Dominion to the different provinces. The population of Ontario has vastly increased since 1861, but we get no increase in our subsidy. The province of Quebec has increased largely in population since 1861, but the province of Quebec gets no increase in subsidy, while the province qf Prince Edward Island gets an increase in its subsidy every ten years according to the increase in its population. Therefore, I say, not only in the annual grant for government purposes, has Prince Edward Island had a preference ever since she came into confederation, but in the payment of the subsidy she has a preference over the other two provinces. In this way, I contend, that the province of Prince Edward Island has already been very largely compensated for the loss that she has sustained under the agreement made at the time she came into confederation. However, a grievance appears to exist; the people of Prince Edward Island contend that there is money owing to them, the government have considered this matter no doubt very fully and they have

come to the conclusion, that it had better be settled. I am not prepared at this moment to say what would be a proper amount, whether $30,000 per annum or $20,000 per annum, but I am inclined to think at the very outset that the figure which has been named is abundantly sufficient, and I infer that possibly the political exigencies of the matter have induced the government to arrive at the conclusion that the larger figure is the figure that they should propose to pay to Prince Edward Island. I am glad however that the government have adopted the plan qf paying this sum, whatever it is to be, whether $20,000 per year or $30,000 per year, as an annual subsidy instead of giving the province a bulk sum of money. I think it would have been a bad thing indeed if this sum had been capitalized and the province of Prince Edward Island had been handed over $1,000,000 instead of $30,000 a year. We in Ontario know how our finances have been squandered owing to the fact that the subsidy granted in 1884 has been treated by the Ontario government, not as a subsidy, but as interest on the capital sum and then drawing from the Dominion government a loan against that sum, hypothecating, or mortgaging the capitalized sum of the subsidy. We know in Ontario how our entire trust funds have been wasted and dissipated. Whereas, at the time of confederation we had trust moneys invested and in the hands of the Dominion government to the extent of about $3,500,000 and we got an increased subsidy in 1884 of $142,000, yet notwithstanding that, we are to-day, I may say, without a single dollar of surplus, although the treasurer of the province of Ontario comes down year after year and tells the people he has a surplus of some $2,500,000, a conclusion which he arrives at by simply capitalizing the subsidy of 1884.

I hope that the government will go a little further and that they will grant this subsidy on such conditions that the province of Prince Edward Island cannot possibly hypothecate or mortgage it in any form, so that it will remain for ever a subsidy, and that they never can be able to draw from the Dominion treasury the capitalized sum, or yet borrow from the Dominion government and pledge the subsidy as security. I believe that condition to be essential if we are going to keep the province out of debt. It is a great question to-day as to what is going to become of the different provincial governments. They are rapidly getting into debt and the Federal government will of necessity require to exercise some paternal care over them, because when they get involved beyond redemption you can rest assured they will come to the Dominion government to help them out of their difficulty. If we are entering the thin end of the wedge, if we are again opening up the question of subsidies to the provinces, we should surround it with safeguards that will prevent these subsidies from being dissipated and wasted. We should see to it that the money shall be used for nothing but the ordinary purposes of government from year to year, and thereby reserve for future generations the revenue for the provinces, and not have Prince Edward Island coming back some years hence asking us for something additional. I trust that in the Bill to be founded on these resolutions there will be some safeguard that will prevent as far as possible the extravagant expenditure of this grant.

,Independent Conservative,,William Findlay Maclean,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06cf61a5-7c95-4155-ab94-d0d4156924b9&Language=E&Section=ALL

CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,I take this opportunity of saying that not only do I not write in La Patrie-I have no time to do so-but often I am a week and more without reading it. I may say, however, that before I came into the Chamber to-night I read the article to which reference has been made. La Patrie has published an article from L'Evenement of Quebec, a Conservative paper. It is a dangerous proceeding. I may say at once that I altogether differ from the sentiments expressed in that article. The province of Quebec is quite capable of going on without the aid of this parliament. The province of Quebec has no claim, and does not mean to have any claim, against this Dominion. It is a false impression that the province of Quebec -is more in debt than the other provinces are. It may appear that way to those who do not know the real facts of the case. The debt of the province of Quebec is pretty large but our municipal debt is small, while the municipal debt of the province of Ontario is very large. I say that the province of Quebec has no claim against the Dominion. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) has said that the province of Quebec is going to make a

raid on the Dominion treasury, and you will see it in the Toronto World in the morning under big headings. X want to tell the House and the country that there is nothing in that statement, and that the province of Quebec is quite capable of standing on its own legs. I contend that we are not opening the door in any way here, but that we are simply settling an account which should have been settled long ago, as we are settling other accounts which should have been settled long ago. The provinces should not expect from the Dominion anything more than they are receiving now. I, of course, speak for myself alone, but I think that ail those who have given some attention to the affairs of this Dominion are prepared to take the stand that the provinces should learn to know that they must govern themselves according to tl'eir means. If they spend more than they should do, let them pay the tax. The Dominion is one thing and the provinces are another.

,,,The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS.,
19249,ca.proc.d.1901-05-08.12.33,1901-05-08,0161da2d-c63a-468c-a51e-070c1f9ee40f,ca.m.3700,Hon. JOHN HAGGART (South Lanark).,,P.E.I. CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,I have no great objection to the amount of money which is to be given to Prince Edward Island, but if there is to be a readjustment let it be all around. The Minister of Public Works says that this is a just claim and that it ought to have been settled long ago. How does he know it was not settled long ago ? How does he know that in the readjustment of 1884, Prince Edward Island was not settled with ? The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine say that all these claims had accrued in 1887, but was not the sum granted in 1887 to Prince Edward Island a settlement in full? I remember that when we gave that $20,000 extra to Prince Edward Island it was supposed to be in satisfaction of all claims which were not allowed in 1884. The claim now is, that under the terms of the union in 1873, we were obliged to give an efficient service to Prince Edward Island, and that we failed. It is rather curious to find this Liberal government finding fault with the service which was in existence between 1874 and 1878. They were in power then, and their Minister of Marine in the Mackenzie government built the Northern Light. Again and again we have heard them strenuously defend that vessel, and state in this House that she performed all the conditions required by the terms of the union. Even Sir Louis Davies, after he got into power, admitted that the services of the Northern Light were most efficient, except during a few weeks in the year, and that, from an inquiry by a committee of the House, and from his own knowledge of all the facts known to science at that day, there were no means by which, for four or six weeks in the winter, communication could be kept up. These are the facts of the case. If you want to give a larger Mr. TARTE.

subsidy to Prince Edward Island, if you want to make up for the misgovernment of that province from 1891 to 1901, by which it has lost an amount equal to $1,000,000, or the $30,000 per annum which you are giving it, give the money on some principle which will be just and fair to the other provinces, but not for the reasons which the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries assign-th4Tt from 1874 to 1878 the contract was not carried out in accordance with the terms of the treaty. I have heard these hon. gentlemen again and again defend the action of the government in carrying out that contract. From 1878 to 1887, I have heard them justify the employment of every vessel which was employed to perform the contract. I have heard the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, from his place in the House, say that all the requirements of the contract were performed by the Northern Light except for four or six weeks. How have we performed the conditions ? In the first place, years after the province entered the union, there was a net loss to the Dominion of $15,000 a year in carrying out the contract, and for the succeeding years, up to the present time, we have had a net loss of $20,000 a year, and an expenditure of over $400,000 on boats, besides annual grants made to different steamship companies in Charlottetown for the purpose of supplementing the service. We have done our very utmost to perform the contract; and what a farce it is to come here at the present time and ask for $30,000 a year as compensation for conditions which it is claimed have not been performed by the Dominion. I say the Dominion has -performed to the utmost letter every promise it made to Prince Edward Island; and if the island, as I believe it did, entered confederation without having determined its financial position in a proper manner-because I do not think it got justice in coming into confederation-and if it is entitled to a further sum, let the settlement be made on a fair basis, showing the reasons therefor; but, do not come down with apologies such as those given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for a further grant. If there was injustice done when the little island came into confederation, there is no man in the Dominion, from one end to the other, who is not proud of its acquisition as a part of this great Dominion, and who will not be prepared to do it justice to the utmost ; but if you are going to increase any of the provincial subsidies, people from one end of the Dominion to the other will insist that, at the same time, justice be done to all the provinces ; and if there are to be increased subsidies to New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island because they have equitable claims on the Dominion of Canada, my own province has more equitable claims ten times over than any of the provinces by the sea.

CLAIMS-MAINTENANCE OF STEAM COMMUNICATION.,,,Mr. Speaker, I wish to add just a word to what has been said by the hon. Minister of Public Works. Each time a province comes before this government to ask, not for a readjustment of subsidy, but for the settlement of claims, it is the custom for certain papers to say that there will be a raid from the province of Quebec on the Dominion exchequer. Well, Mr. Speaker, although 1 am a young man, I have followed the politics of my own province during the last ten or fifteen years, and I must say that the province of Quebec, as it stands to-day, is well able to take care of itself. Under the administration of the Hon. Mr. Marchand, and the present administration as led by Hon. Mr. Parent, the government of the province of Quebec has been able, during the last four or five years, to show very good surpluses existing in reality ; and these surpluses are a demonstration that the government of Quebec is wisely administered. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the claim of the province of Prince Edward Island has been well put before the House, and the argument which was presented to Lord Granville ten or twelve years ago, when the claim of Prince Edward Island was placed at the foot of the Throne by the delegates from that province, is the justification of the Dominion government in the course they have adopted. About the question of readjustment of provincial subsidies, I may add that while I am not in a position this evening to advocate such a readjustment, I must say that it is not a party question, either in the different provinces or in this Dominion parliament. This question has been studied by the governments of the different provinces since confederation. Speaking for my own province, I may say that even in 1883, the Conservative party in Quebec, led by the Hon. Mr. Wurtele, who is now Mr. Justice Wurtele of the Appeal Court, at that time Treasurer of the provincial government, in his budget speech, made a claim on the Federal government for a readjustment of subsidies, and he gave very good reasons for it. Later on, the Hon. Mr. Mousseau, who after being Secretary of State in the Dominion government, became afterwards premier of the province of Quebec, made also one of the chief planks of his platform, in the session of 1884, this question of the readjustment of provincial subsidies. Later on, in 1887, the question came up before the Quebec interprovincial conference, and it was taken up by public men, not only from the province of Quebec, but from all the provinces there represented.

Mr. Ross, then Treasurer of the province of Ontario. At that conference all the provinces were represented. That this conference is of opinion that a basis for a final and unalterable settlement of the amounts to be yearly paid by the Dominion to the several provinces for their local purposes, and the support of their governments and legislatures may be found in the proposal following, that Is to say

Then, axe recited the different grievances and the schedule of yearly payments that should be added to the provincial subsidies. This only goes to show that this claim for the readjustment of provincial subsidies, or what some federalists call raids on the Federal exchequer, did not come from the 'province of Quebec. Such questions are discussed in the province of Quebec just as well as in the other provinces ; and when I find that the province of Ontario adopted the resolutions of the interprovincial conference, I am inclined to say that surely this question must be a very important one, worthy of the consideration of this House and country. Why should we avoid a discussion of such an interesting question ? It is well known to-day that the circumstances under which the provinces joined confederation are no longer the same. We receive, as the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) said, a moment ago, a yearly subvention of 80 cents per head, based on the census of 1861. Well, at the time that this amount was granted to the provinces, it was considered that it would be sufficient to meet the cost of the administration of justice and the maintenance of jails and other services. But it is fairly demonstrated to-day that the population has increased considerably, especially in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The circumstances have completely changed, and as the old English proverb puts it, 'Circumstances alter cases.' This question can very fairly be considered, I repeat. Every true friend of this confederation and of the Dominion parliament should be in sympathy with provincial sentiments and aspirations. The provinces were constituted to live and not to die, and it is the duty of the Federal government to protect them. It has been said that they have gone deeply into debt. To a certain extent that may be true. True

it is that in Quebec we have a large debt of about .$25,000,000 or $30,000,000 ; but, as the hon. Minister of Public Works has said, if we have a large public debt, the interest on it is regularly paid, and it is a debt which the financiers of London were pleased to increase when we made a call on them. It must not be forgotten also that we have in the province of Quebec practically no municipal debt, which cannot be said of some of the other provinces. The province of Quebec has taken hold of certain public works, which the other provinces would not undertake, but left them to be done by the municipalities. Those were outside the ordinary administration of our affairs, with respect to which we stand on an equal footing as compared with the other provinces. I did not intend to make a speech this evening on a readjustment of the subsidies, but I say that we should not be afraid to face that question fairly. It is an open question, and one which it is fitting we should discuss, because the provinces are entitled to some consideration in this compact of confederation. column1: I presume it will not be necessary to go over tbe reasons why it is desirable to have a standard measure for fruit. Hon. gentlemen will observe in reading this Bill that we have a standard measure for almost everything that is sold, for all kinds of grain, vegetables, apples, barrels of salt, potatoes and even bundles of hay, but there is no standard size for a basket of fruit. A fruit basket originally was supposed to contain 12 quarts. The growers found the 12-quart size to be about the right size, as it was the largest size in which fruit could be conveniently sent to market. They adopted that size, but the size not being legalized, gradually diminished because there were dishonest men who wished to take advantage of the fact that the consumer could not tell easily the difference between an 11-quart and a 12-quart basket. The size fell until to-day there are proportionately more ten and a half quart baskets than twelve quart baskets, which is a great injustice to the honest shipper who wishes to ship in a standard basket. A similar condition prevails in regard to berry boxes. As I said when this Bill received a second reading, I do not think there is at the present time much dishonesty in the shipping of berries by the growers, but there is a great injustice done to growers by dealers in the

large cities who buy these berries in regular standard boxes and before they reach the market they transfer them to smaller boxes and retail them out in smaller boxes to the consumers, the consumers believing they are getting the ordinary sized boxes.
